newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro readies privatisation of power industry.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro readies privatisation of power industry.

text.p: The privatisation of Montenegro's power industry is the only way to meet consumer needs and update obsolete technology, economists said on Monday.

"The electric power industry does not have to be state property to regularly provide electricity to its citizens," Veselin Vukotic, in charge of the Montenegrin power industry reform, told Reuters in an interview.
"Providing electricity is of public interest and the form of ownership (of the industry) has nothing to do with that," said Vukotic, also professor at the Podgorica School of Economics.
The Yugoslav republic of Montenegro, set on the path of market economy, has urged privatisation of its key utilities.
It has commissioned evaluations and forms of privatisation of the country's electric power industry as well as the post and telecommunications company.

Privatisation is the only way to attract the foreign investment needed to upgrade outdated public utilities hit by four years of international sanctions and shortage of cash, another Montenegrin economist said.
The team of more than hundred reasearchers have finalised the first part of a power industry reform study, setting the total value of the electricity power sector at $1.2 billion.
The figure includes the value of two hydro-electric power plants and one thermal power plant, a system of seven small hydro-electric power stations and the entire transmission and distribution grid.
Vukotic could not tell if that was the true value, but added: "That is how much it would be worth if electricity here would have the same price as in the world."
Vukotic said electricity cost about 40 percent less in Montenegro than in western Europe.
He said the study treated electricity as commodity and that the $1.2 billion would be used as a base figure for the industry's privatisation.
"The second part of the study laying out a concrete model for the sector's privatisation will be finished by the end of 1997," Vukotic said.

Unlike Montenegro, Serbia has taken a more cautious approach to privatisation but early in August news leaked that the Serbian government had commissioned NatWest Markets of Britain to launch privatisation of the parts of its PTT company.
